set.stem: A 75-year-old smoker with ischaemic heart disease and previous heart failure presents with a 6-hour history of palpitations and increasing breathlessness. He is alert, BP 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 94% on air, with no chest pain, and his chest is clear. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 160/min, and vagal manoeuvres have had no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Slow the heart rate with IV atenolol to help identify the rhythm
IV lidocaine 50 mg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 mg/min
IV adenosine to terminate the rhythm or reveal the underlying atrial activity
Immediate DC cardioversion, because the rhythm may be ventricular tachycardia
Withhold oxygen because he is a smoker
set.explanation: For a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal manoeuvres are followed by rapid IV adenosine (6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg): it terminates AV-node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT, AVRT), and if the rhythm is atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia the transient AV block unmasks the atrial activity and confirms the diagnosis. A narrow QRS makes VT very unlikely, lidocaine has no role in supraventricular rhythms, and IV beta-blockade before a diagnosis is made risks worsening his heart failure. Synchronised cardioversion is reserved for adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, severe heart failure), and oxygen is titrated to target saturations rather than withheld.

why: Added haemodynamic stability, a clear chest and failed vagal manoeuvres so that adenosine is the single best answer (with adverse features, cardioversion would be indicated)

set.stem: A 57-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of a strong family history of heart disease. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with a constant PR interval of 300 ms (0.3 s), and every P wave is followed by a QRS complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A PR interval longer than 200 ms (five small squares) with every P wave conducted is first-degree AV block. It reflects slowed AV-nodal conduction (ageing and fibrosis, high vagal tone, beta-blockers, digoxin, verapamil, inferior MI) and needs no treatment in isolation. In Mobitz I the PR lengthens progressively until a beat is dropped, in Mobitz II some P waves are blocked without prior PR change, and in complete heart block the atria and ventricles beat independently; sick sinus syndrome causes sinus pauses and brady–tachy episodes rather than a long PR.

why: Same idea as arr-0097 (older patient with AF and an enlarged left atrium: rate control plus long-term anticoagulation rather than cardioversion)

set.stem: You are the junior doctor on call and a nurse asks you to review an ECG. It shows regular P waves with a constant PR interval in the conducted beats, but some P waves are not followed by a QRS complex; there is no progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beats. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Intermittently non-conducted P waves with a fixed PR interval in the conducted beats is Mobitz type II second-degree AV block. The block is usually infranodal (His–Purkinje system), often with a broad QRS, and can progress abruptly to complete heart block, so permanent pacing is indicated. In Mobitz I (Wenckebach) the PR lengthens progressively before the dropped beat and the block is usually nodal and benign, while in complete heart block there is no relationship at all between P waves and QRS complexes.

why: Same idea as arr-0008 (independent P waves and QRS complexes, i.e. AV dissociation with a slow rate = complete heart block)
Same idea as arr-0093 (shockable cardiac arrest, VF or pulseless VT, is treated first with an immediate defibrillation shock)

set.stem: At an ECG teaching session, a consultant describes a patient admitted to the coronary care unit with a regular atrial rate of 300/min and a regular ventricular rate of 150/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: An atrial rate of about 300/min with exactly half of the impulses conducted is typical atrial flutter with 2:1 AV block: a macro-re-entrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus produces sawtooth flutter waves, best seen in II, III, aVF and V1. Any regular narrow-complex tachycardia at close to 150/min should raise suspicion of 2:1 flutter; vagal manoeuvres or adenosine increase the block and reveal the flutter waves. The heart-block options describe slow ventricular rates with normal atrial rates, not an atrial rate of 300/min.

set.stem: A patient on the coronary care unit develops new atrial flutter with an atrial rate of 300/min and a ventricular rate of 150/min; it began about 6 hours ago. He is haemodynamically stable, and a rhythm-control strategy is chosen. What is the most effective first-line treatment to restore sinus rhythm?
set.explanation: Atrial flutter is restored to sinus rhythm by low-energy synchronised DC cardioversion in more than 90% of cases, far more reliably than with drugs; with onset within the last 24–48 hours it can be performed once anticoagulation has been started, and thromboembolic precautions are the same as for AF. Class I drugs such as procainamide or flecainide convert flutter poorly and may slow the flutter rate enough to allow 1:1 conduction, and sotalol mainly slows the rate and is used for maintenance. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is the definitive treatment for recurrent typical flutter rather than the acute step, and lidocaine is used only for ventricular arrhythmias.

why: Stem now states the onset, haemodynamic stability and the chosen rhythm-control strategy, so cardioversion is the single best answer; lignocaine renamed lidocaine

set.stem: A previously well 36-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of attacks of palpitations and sweating. The attacks come on suddenly and are unrelated to food, posture or exercise. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Which of the following investigations is the LEAST useful in evaluating her?
set.explanation: Paroxysmal palpitations with sweating in a young woman should be investigated for thyrotoxicosis (thyroid function tests), phaeochromocytoma (plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines), an arrhythmia captured on ambulatory ECG (Holter or event recorder) and structural heart disease (echocardiography). An upper gastrointestinal contrast study has no role, because the attacks are unrelated to food and she has no gastrointestinal symptoms.

why: Same idea as arr-0109 (a beta-blocker such as bisoprolol for rate control of stable AF)

set.stem: A 37-year-old woman develops palpitations after recent surgery. Her pulse is regular at 175/min and BP is 125/70 mmHg; she is otherwise well. She has asthma. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
set.explanation: A haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia (most likely AVNRT) is treated first with vagal manoeuvres – a modified Valsalva manoeuvre or, in a young patient without a carotid bruit, carotid sinus massage. Adenosine would normally be next, but it can cause bronchospasm and is best avoided in asthma; IV verapamil is then the drug of choice if vagal manoeuvres fail. DC cardioversion is reserved for adverse features, and flecainide is not a first-line acute treatment.

set.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after collapsing during football training. He is now alert and orientated, and his vital signs and examination are normal. He remembers feeling dizzy before collapsing but recalls little else. He is normally healthy and takes no regular medication. Blood tests have been sent. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: Syncope during exertion in a young athlete is a red flag for a cardiac cause – hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, Brugada syndrome, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy or an anomalous coronary artery – and a 12-lead ECG is the essential first test in every patient with syncope. Echocardiography, exercise testing, ambulatory monitoring and cardiology review follow, and he should not return to sport until cleared. EEG and neurology review are for suspected seizures, and tilt testing is for suspected reflex syncope, which typically occurs after rather than during exercise.

set.stem: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old man presents to his GP with palpitations and is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse. The episode lasts less than 2 hours in total and resolves without treatment. Full blood count, biochemistry, thyroid function, ECG and echocardiogram are all normal. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
set.explanation: This is a brief, self-terminating episode of probable paroxysmal AF in a man with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0 and a structurally normal heart, so his stroke risk is low and anticoagulation is not recommended. Antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel, dipyridamole) are not recommended for stroke prevention in AF at any score, because they are much less effective than anticoagulants yet still cause bleeding. He needs advice about triggers such as alcohol, ambulatory monitoring if episodes recur, and periodic reassessment of stroke risk.

set.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the coronary care unit with unstable angina and started on appropriate antiplatelet and anti-anginal therapy. She has hypertension; fasting glucose is normal and total cholesterol is 5.2 mmol/L. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate treatment to reduce her risk of stroke?
set.explanation: Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 (age 75 or over 2, female 1, hypertension 1, vascular disease 1), so oral anticoagulation is indicated; antiplatelet therapy, even dual, is much less effective than anticoagulation for AF-related stroke. After an ACS in a patient with AF, guidelines give a short period of triple therapy (anticoagulant plus aspirin plus clopidogrel, usually no more than a week), then anticoagulant plus clopidogrel for up to 12 months and then anticoagulant alone, preferring a DOAC to warfarin. Digoxin only controls the rate, and cardioversion does not remove the need for anticoagulation.

why: Anticoagulant option updated to DOAC or warfarin in line with current ESC guidance; stem clarified that the question concerns stroke prevention
Same idea as arr-0064 (stable SVT not terminated by carotid sinus massage is treated with IV adenosine)

set.stem: A 29-year-old woman sees her GP with fatigue, palpitations and weight loss without dieting. Her pulse is about 120/min and irregularly irregular, BP 142/89 mmHg and BMI 19 kg/m2; there are no added heart sounds. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most useful next investigation?
set.explanation: Weight loss without dieting, fatigue, a low BMI and new AF in a young woman strongly suggest hyperthyroidism, so thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4) are the key next test; TFTs are recommended for everyone with new AF. Thyrotoxic AF is rate-controlled with a beta-blocker such as propranolol and often reverts once the patient is euthyroid. A repeat ECG adds nothing, and a chest X-ray, full blood count or glucose would not explain the whole picture.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction presents with palpitations that began 3 hours ago; this is his first known episode. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 130/min without acute ischaemic changes. He has mild central chest discomfort, but BP is 128/80 mmHg and he is not distressed. A rhythm-control strategy is preferred. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Heparin and digoxin at the standard daily dose
Heparin followed by synchronised DC cardioversion
Wait for spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm
set.explanation: AF of recent onset (within 24–48 hours) can be cardioverted once anticoagulation with heparin or a DOAC has been started, without prior transoesophageal echocardiography. Because he has had an MI (structural heart disease), flecainide is contraindicated, so electrical cardioversion (or IV amiodarone) is the rhythm-control option. A beta-blocker combined with verapamil risks profound bradycardia, hypotension and heart failure, digoxin is slow and does not restore sinus rhythm, and a wait-and-see approach suits only patients who are asymptomatic with a controlled rate. Long-term anticoagulation afterwards depends on his CHA2DS2-VASc score, not on the success of cardioversion.

why: Added prior MI (excluding flecainide), haemodynamic stability and a chosen rhythm-control strategy; the cardioversion option now includes anticoagulation first
The same question as arr-0093 (pulseless VT: defibrillation first), reprinted in another source
Same idea as arr-0064 (stable narrow-complex tachycardia after failed vagal manoeuvres: IV adenosine)
Same idea as arr-0009 (AF with shock: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion)

set.stem: A 69-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and asthma is evaluated. Episodes are infrequent, and echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart. Which statement regarding her management is correct?
options: Digoxin effectively prevents recurrences of the arrhythmia
Sotalol is a suitable choice to prevent recurrences
Oral flecainide taken as needed may be an effective way to terminate an attack
set.explanation: With infrequent paroxysms and no structural or ischaemic heart disease, a single oral dose of flecainide (200–300 mg) taken at the onset of symptoms, the pill-in-the-pocket approach, can terminate attacks; it is first tried under monitoring and combined with an AV-nodal blocker (verapamil or diltiazem when a beta-blocker is unsuitable). Sotalol is a non-selective beta-blocker and is contraindicated in asthma, digoxin does not prevent paroxysms, and amiodarone is toxic long term but not contraindicated. Paroxysmal AF carries a stroke risk similar to persistent AF, and at age 65–74 anticoagulation should at least be considered, so it cannot be dismissed as unnecessary.

why: Added a structurally normal heart and infrequent episodes, which the pill-in-the-pocket option requires; distractors reworded as clear statements

set.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of shortness of breath. His pulse is irregular at 140/min, and the ECG shows atrial fibrillation. What would you expect to see in the jugular venous pulse?
set.explanation: The a wave of the JVP is produced by right atrial contraction; in atrial fibrillation there is no coordinated atrial systole, so a waves are absent. Cannon a waves occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (complete heart block, VT, junctional rhythms), large a waves with tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary stenosis, and large v waves with tricuspid regurgitation.

why: Same idea as arr-0066 (first-degree AV block = PR interval over 200 ms)
